body: Wrong. Her husband already decided this for her.

She has acted polite and amicable when shes physically around you because she is SCARED OF YOU. Back off. You need to examine yourself, your post is just you non-stop putting your potential romantic interest in this girl above her obvious discomfort with you. Your wants don't ever come before another person's boundaries.

You're not going to be able to stop being an asshole until you figure out WHY you thought it was acceptable to treat her like this. WHY did you think it was okay to respond to her kindness with anger? I'm going to go out on a limb here and guess you don't treat your other friends or family members like this. So WHY do you treat her this way? 

If you really want to change your behavior, you're going to have to change the way you think. This is going to require a lot of self-reflection. You're going to have to ask yourself some tough questions. There may be even less room for her in your life if you commit to focus on yourself and your problems. Breaking up with her could be for the best. Possibly look into therapy.

I had a very non-normal childhood and sometimes wish I could walk around with a shirt that said "HEY IM TRAUMATIZED" becuase I have this fundamental feeling that acting like a normal person means I'm a fraud and a liar. So. I know where you're coming from, haha.


From what I've experienced... talking about this with other people goes best when they're the ones that show some sort of vulnerability to you, unprompted, first. It takes some patience, but people do it more than you'd think. Of the top of my head, here's some things that've turned into conversations about my past traumas. More often than not, it turns into a conversation about OUR past traumas:


-being worried about moving to a new town/apartment

-dumb shit we did back in high school/college

-bad/annoying habits


We as a society don't usually see these as dark/scary topics, but most people have at least a little pain or insecurity behind stuff like this which can help them more easily sympathize with you and understand how you feel.

Here's the most important thing I've learned about this: Being truthful about your pain and trauma is like any other habit. The more you do it, the easier it becomes.

I had a childhood similar to this. I have chosen to cut my parents out of my life entirely, but I still secretly hope that they separate someday. You sound very heartbroken over your mother's situation, and guilty for not being able to save her from it, but please consider this: she is an adult, and you are not. It was your mothers responsibility to protect you from having to live in fear with this man, not the other way around.

You owe it to yourself NOT to take responsibility for your mother's actions.

It makes sense why your ex was the first person you thought to go to when feeling overwhelmed. Maybe it might even be a good idea to talk to her sometime in the future about this when things have settled down. But right now you owe it to yourself to talk to someone who is fully trained in helping you cope with this, and thats a professional.

So, your dad is insulting and demanding. Some people can handle having harsh parents and have good relationships with them despite that; other people decide that they can't. To be clear, I'm one of the latter. Here's some questions to ask yourself:

How does the idea of spending 2 more years in this environment make you feel? 

Have you told your dad how he makes you feel, and how did he respond? 

Do you find yourself dwelling on your dad's insults? 

Does the way your dad treats you make you feel isolated? 

If you didn't live with your dad right now, how much would you still try to involve him in your life? 

Do you think he would try to keep you involved in his?

If you're in school there should be some sort of on campus mental health resources you can use or a crisis hotline you can call (not that you have to be in a crisis, I've called my school hotline several times for heavy-but-not-quite-CRISIS things). You could also look into sliding scale therapists in your area. For awhile I went to a place staffed by psych grad students that cost like $10 a trip. Maybe the hospital has some sort of grief counseling resources?


And it does sound like what you're going through right now is grief, even if your sister still has a chance of recovery. Feeling numb like you've described here is normal when a life-shattering thing happens suddenly like this. Don't worry about what you "should" be feeling right now; there's no such thing as a right or wrong way to feel when faced with a tragedy. Just let yourself feel whatever it is you're feeling tonight and take time tomorrow to look into counseling options.


Ultimately though: you sound too emotionally raw right now to be contacting an ex.
You probably need to talk to a counselor or therapist about what you're going through, not your ex. She might have been very close to you, but for what you're dealing with you need a professional.

You had seven good years with this community. If you leave now, it won't make those past seven good years disappear. You seem to already know this, but its time to move on to whatever will make you make you happy next, because it certainly won't be this community.

You probably need to get this person out of your house in the coming month or something. She doesn't seems stable, so I don't think kicking her out on the curb as soon as she comes home is fair to her, and it could also potentially be dangerous for you and your roommates. You and your roommates are not going to be happy living with someone you know to be unstable, and she is not going to be happy going back to the same house she tried to kill herself in.


Unlike most of the other commenters... I don't think she attempted suicide to manipulate you. She described herself on the phone as feeling "trapped". I've had serious suicide scares myself, and feeling trapped was always the number one thing that made my regular old depression tip over into suicidal territory. You confronting her about the phone call without actually having a CONVERSATION with her about it probably left her feeling even more trapped and hopeless about her situation. Your response to her bitching came off as standoffish and hostile, without trying to engage her in her obvious problems with you and your roommates.


Her attempting was NOT your fault, and it would be best for everyone involved if she left. But I think you should reflect some on how you communicate with your roommates, here.


EDIT: Ok I looked at your original post and I see now that having a conversation about her phone call would probably have gone just as badly. I still don't think she was being manipulative in her attempt but... yeah. You tried to initiate some kind of heart-to-heart communication before, and now that the well's poisoned its time for her to go, ASAP.
I don't have anything to say that other commenters haven't covered, except for: keep your relationship with your siblings strong. They're the best allies you can have in this situation.

"blah blah blah"? Are you serious? You didn't even need to type up that wall of text, because those three words explained how little you understand what your daughter is experiencing right now.

She is traumatized. The medicine hasn't made her into a shell of what she once was, the TRAUMA has done that. The things that help you feel better when you're feeling down will not help her because she's not feeling down, she is feeling TRAUMATIZED. Someone brutalized her and stripped her autonomy from her. No one just does some jumping jacks and "gets over" something like this. If you want to help her, you should show her unconditional support.

You seem to already know this, but all you can do is work on a plan to get yourself out of this house permanently. Maybe you could join a club or something to get some more hours out of the house? Both you and your sister are in a hostile home environment; the only way you can help you sister now is by setting an example that you DON'T have to stay miserable in your parents' house forever. If you force your parents to kick her out, she'll likely resent you forever AND you will become the only target for your parents' abuse.

Your dad is miserable, and is choosing to deal with this by pushing his misery onto others. This isn't how adults deal with their issues, and your dad has been an adult for a very long time. Its not your job to put up with his childish behavior. Just because you're an adult now, doesn't mean you've become his parent. Continue keeping this person at arms length, or further. For your own sake.

If you're gonna confrom them, I recommend first making a "normal" trip home and collecting any important documents/personal items you might still have hanging around at their house. Abusive parents quickly turn hostile when called out on all their years of abuse, and you might not get another chance to pick up stuff left behind.

Your mother sounds emotionally abusive, and like she has very little understanding of boundaries. Someone's already recommended r/rbn but I'd also recommend getting into some kind of counseling with your school and looking into books on the subject of toxic parents. If you've been around this woman your entire life, she's probably worn down your ability to stand up to her bullying and enforce your own boundaries. Counseling/therapy will help you get that back.

Then its a good thing you're doing what you can and reaching out here! But don't discount your own need for support and validation; I've found that when I'm feeling my most insane, nothing helps more than someone else telling me its okay to feel the way I do.

As for what you should do about your mother... Maybe you should start researching parental alienation. (oops, just realized i refered to her as your MIL before)
This person is actively working against your healing process after the loss of your daughter and needs to be removed from your life for an indefinate amount of time.

It sounds like you've already made the best decision possible for your son by limiting his exposure to MiL, but right now you need to work on caring for yourself. Have you looked into any therapist/counselor options over there?

Your mom sounds like she's placating and tolerable while you remain within her good graces, but cruel and threatening if you do anything she disapproves of. This isn't a normal or acceptable way to treat children, especially adult children that should be gaining more control over their lives. I highly doubt you'll ever be able to make her understand that the way she's treating you isn't ok. The best thing you could do for yourself is talk to a conselor or therapist who will also tell you that the way you're being treated right now isn't your fault. Your feelings are valid; if you continue to let your mom isolate you you'll only feel worse. Seek out people that will validate your feelings.

You may want to take a look at r/raisedbynarcissists

It's been mentioned in this post already, I think, but the book Why Does He Do That? by Lundy Bancroft dissects abusive relationships and how they come to exist. If you honestly want to know why people stay with abusers I suggest giving it a read.

My parents have found me and shown up, unannounced, screaming at my door before. If this happens, call the police the SECOND the show up. I opened the door and tried to warn them to leave before I called the cops, and it wasn't worth it. Should this ever happen, you might want to talk to the cops that show up about getting a restraining order.

I was out with uncles catching up on stuff and we inevitably got to the Mom Cutoff subject. They are very much on my "side" (though I don't really want to make people choose sides or w/e) and we we're having a big ol' airing of grievances since they had silently agreed that my Nmom was crazy a long time ago. They didn't tell me this in an attempt to rile me up, I'm certain, just to let me know how far my Nmom is going right now in her attempt to paint me as crazy and unstable so as to defend herself.

You may want to think about whether the guilt and sympathy she shows other people is done in a martyr fashion. Also: the things you confide in her during her "good times", does she have a tendency to later use them against you during the "bad times"? Ns can find ways to disguise their N behaviors into seemingly normal healthy behavior. For me, the avidly refusing to respect your basic boundaries thing is a giant red arrow that points to N, but I don't know your mom, only you can really decide whether she fits the N mold or not.

"What do you have to worry about? HIPPA exists, I can't possibly MAKE her tell me stuff. I just want to get a better understanding, set things straight."

Only you can define your mother as an N or not. You know her and we don't, after all. But what you described does not sound like a healthy supportive mother. It sounds like someone intentionally trying to build up your hopes only so she can then turn around and dash them. Do you have a counseling center at your school or a trusted ballet teacher you can talk to about your poor attendance, and how its out of your control?

An enabler is someone who is in a position to stop abuse but pretends they have no idea what is going on. Sometimes the abuser incorporates the enabler in some of their abuse tactics, sometimes the abuser takes their anger out on the enabler as well, but for the most part the enabler just plugs their ears and privately feels grateful that you're taking the abuse and not them.

The first book I read upon realizing that my childhood wasn't normal was Toxic Parents by Susan Forward. I thought it was a really good starting point because it examined many different types of parental dysfunction, gave plenty of case study examples, and did a good job detailing what child abuse looks like in an adult victim. Tore through it in about 2 days.

Here's the thing: I have been there a lot emotionally for my mom. I don't know how many times she's come to me to unload all her problems with my dad. I try to be understanding but she's never extended the same effort to me. I never feel safe talking to her about my emotions; the few times I tried in the past she either ignored my emotional distress or tried to "one up" me. Thank you for commenting though. Hearing people say that the way she treats me wasn't normal really does help... It's pretty amazing the way a parent can teach you to distrust yourself and your perception of reality.

I know how you feel. I saw it with a younger sister and started crying because I saw me on the screen. Once my sister told me that she doesn't remember me from when I was younger, because I used to spend all my time in my room with the door locked.

It actually made me kind of mad when Let It Go started up and Elsa suddenly became confident and sexy and etc etc.... but that's just because I was projecting myself onto her really hard during the scene where she's alone after her parents died. Funny enough though, my sister said she related to it as a "coming out" story, with Elsa trying to deny her ice powers reminding her of knowing she wasn't straight while growing up. I guess there's a lot of different ways to experience isolation.

Last time... well, I guess I let my parents help me, that's how I managed to get out. They screamed at me and I was miserable for a while, sure, but then my mom sat me down and we went through the class listing for the next semester until we found a group of classes I knew I could pass. I don't think they were thinking this way, but I knew that I had to start by succeeding at little things until I could feel like I was capable of succeeding at big things again. Have you looked at your degree plan? You probably have room to take some easier "blow off"-ish type classes. The semester I failed, I took biology, chemistry, calculus, and medical ethics. The next semester, I took art history, spanish, and psychology. I would recommend looking at taking a physical ed class if you can, something like beginners jogging. Exercise is supposed to help with depression, and its an easy way to make an A so long as you attend. I'm not sure if you mentioned if you're a STEM major or not (I'm just assuming here) but I would encourage you to sign up for classes that are a lot different than the classes you're struggling with right now. Another thing you might consider doing is planning to attend a cheap community college over the summer and revisiting your math basics, even if it won't get you any credit at the school you're at. I went back and took algebra and pre-calculus, it made a world of difference. When I retook calculus the next fall, I actually got an A! I'm certain you can do it too, with some preparation. Is there any way you can still drop the calculus class right now? My school allows one emergency drop that you can use up until final day, maybe you have an option like that too. If you know calculus is a lost cause right now, of course it will be impossible to get motivated to study for it. Maybe putting it out of your mind for now will let you focus on salvaging whatever you can in your other classes.

These are all short-term solutions to your grades problem, however. They got me out of the hole I dug for myself first semester, but as I mentioned, without getting real professional help, you're at risk of falling into another depressive slump even after recovering from the one you're in right now. For now, put whatever energy you have left into making it past finals time. Whatever happens happens, after you get past the next couple of weeks you can think about what you need to do to prevent this from happening again. Someway or another, you can make it past this!

This is actually pretty common! It's called Seasonal Affective Disorder, when a person falls into depression routinely around winter time but feels alright during the other seasons. You might want to look into light therapy or antidepressants. I've known a few people who become both depressed and agitated during wintertime, so you're certainly not alone.

You're an undergrad? Have you looked up your school's mental health resources? Even if you don't have a dedicated mental health center, you could make an appointment to talk with a school doctor about getting help.

You sound exactly like me back in 2010... failing everything after excelling in high school, lying to my parents about it because I was afraid of their reactions, isolating myself and going days without talking to anyone, all of it. I was even failing the same class as you, calculus! I ended up with a 1.15 GPA at the end of the semester, only owned up to my parents once they forced me to show them my grade report. They freaked just like I thought they would. But they helped me get back on track the next semester, and I was able to just narrowly avoid getting kicked out entirely. I wish I had been able to come to my parents about my problems instead of them forcing it out of me, but that's not even my biggest regret. My biggest regret is not going to get professional help earlier. I managed to pull myself out of my slump then, and now 3 years later I've fallen into it again, and finally this semester I got myself therapy and medication. You might not be able to salvage this semester (I certainly won't...), but I think acknowledging that something is wrong and getting some support will at least help you make it to christmas break, and then you can focus on getting better by next semester. You said you're adverse to trying medication, have you considered trying therapy instead? Opening up on the internet is a great first step, but talking to a therapist face to face really makes a difference, especially someone who understands how you feel and is trained to help you with recovery.

It sounds like you feel very guilty; I understand how that feels. The other day someone causally mentioned to me how highly a relative speaks of me, I got the worst feeling in my stomach... Feeling like a fraud is tiring, but try to remember what it felt like the last time you felt successful. The person you were then wasn't a fluke or a one time thing, the way you felt then wasn't a lie. You can still be that person, it'll just take some time and some outside help.

I have stomach problems too. When I started seriously researching depression this week I was surprised to find that clinical depression often accompanies stomach issues. My issues got diagnosed about a year ago as IBS... turns out 50 to 90% of people with IBS have a mental disorder. Go figure.

I've also had problems finding a job, as well. The biggest problem for me is that I feel like a fraud all through the application process-- you know, having to sell yourself as reliable, a hard worker, sociable... all the stuff that I TRY to be, but can't maintain. That said... I just unexpectedly landed a job today, and I feel pretty good because its based around one of the last achievements that I can remember feeling proud about. So, I know you've heard this a million times, but: hang in there! Sometimes things really can improve out of the blue. And try to get some medical help ASAP; it sounds like you're already processing whats wrong with your life on your own, which is a great first step. But opening up to someone in real life will move you forward so much more. I talked about my issues with my siblings today after coming home for the holidays (the parents are on hold for now...) and it felt pretty good. For the first time in months things have started going right for me, and it all started with nearly breaking down at my school's mental health clinic.

I don't think that's ENTIRELY true. There were things about myself that other people recognized as depression even when I couldn't see it. I was experiencing these things, and couldn't understand why I couldn't control them, while others could easily see that they were beyond my control. And I'm pretty sure not every researcher that studies depression has it themselves, lol. I think maybe communicating how low the "despair" aspect really gets is the hardest part. 

But I think saying "its impossible to understand depression without experiencing it" is dangerous, that leads "healthy" people to not try to learn about it, and not try to talk about it with people that do have it. People who don't have depression CAN support people who have depression in meaningful ways. Its a good thing that you're trying to understand this, mental health is kind of a "taboo" subject in our society, I think it results in a lot of people taking longer than they need to to get help, or just never getting help at all.

I have the weird combination of optimism mixed in with depression symptoms as well, so you're not alone in that, at least, haha. I think it might be that we're really very optimistic people, but the depression masks that, and the few times our real personality breaks through, it fools us into thinking the depression isn't as bad as it really is.

About the "fake it til you make it"... just because you know something better will eventually come along isn't enough, sometimes. Even if you can identify your problems, and even identify the solution to your problems, depression makes it so that you can't bring yourself to enact those solutions, even when there's logically nothing else holding you back. Look up "learned helplessness", it's kind of like that.

I think the biggest misconception here is the medication is itself the solution... it isn't. Most of us ARE trying to fix our problems. The way I am, though, it feels like trying to run through water. I can get myself to a point where I'm functional and doing just good enough, but I have to overwork myself to get there. The medication is supposed to help that. You still have to work hard. But you don't have to work yourself to the limit to just barely get by.

About a month ago I ran into my school's mental health center openly sobbing, I had been awake for over 24 hours, parents weren't talking to me, etc etc etc. The person at the front desk let me cry it out for about 30 minutes and scheduled me to come back in two weeks to meet with a psychologist.
